considered.teaches: One backend per client type when their needs diverge; the token-handling BFF keeps tokens out of the browser.
considered.title: Backend for frontend
considered.why_not: A single Go gateway is what this run scaffolds; per-client backends are a later refinement you add by hand.

considered.teaches: A sidecar runtime giving portable pub/sub, state and invocation APIs — useful across heterogeneous stacks, extra runtime for a Go-only fleet.
considered.title: Dapr
considered.why_not: This run talks to NATS/Kafka and HTTP directly from Go; Dapr is an additional sidecar runtime nothing here installs.

considered.teaches: No coordinator — each service reacts to the previous fact and emits its own; simple to start, hard to trace past three steps.
considered.title: Saga — choreography
considered.why_not: needs coordination = choreography — you chose orchestration

considered.teaches: With no broker, the orchestrator calls each step over HTTP with an idempotency key and calls the undo endpoints itself on failure.
considered.title: Synchronous compensated call chain
considered.why_not: needs event_backbone = none — you chose nats

considered.teaches: Tail the database log to publish changes — for tables you cannot touch and for parallel runs.
considered.title: Change data capture
considered.why_not: needs migration_approach = parallel-run — you chose strangler

considered.teaches: Separate the write model from a read model shaped for queries — per service, where reads are heavy or their shape fights the writes.
considered.title: CQRS
considered.why_not: needs read_write_model = cqrs — you chose crud

considered.teaches: When sagas outgrow a table and a loop, a workflow engine persists every step for you — Temporal has first-class Go.
considered.title: Durable execution
considered.why_not: This platform generates a saga whose state lives in the orchestrating service’s own database — no extra runtime to operate. Durable execution (Temporal Go SDK) is the upgrade path when flows outgrow it.

considered.teaches: Store the events, derive the state — powerful for audit-heavy domains, a heavy commitment for a port.
considered.title: Event sourcing
considered.why_not: needs read_write_model = event-sourced — you chose crud

considered.teaches: When composition is too slow or too chatty, keep a local copy of the data you read, fed by the owner’s events.
considered.title: Materialized view / read model
considered.why_not: needs read_write_model = cqrs — you chose crud

considered.teaches: Same model, another server — route read-only queries of read-heavy services to a replica and accept its lag.
considered.title: Read replica
considered.why_not: needs at least 1 read_heavy_services — this run has 0

considered.teaches: Remove the read instead of moving it — and replace any package-level cache map, which is per-replica after the split.
considered.title: Read-through cache
considered.why_not: needs at least 1 read_heavy_services — this run has 0

considered.teaches: Reserve, then confirm or cancel — isolation instead of compensation, if every participant can expose the three operations.
considered.title: Try–Confirm–Cancel
considered.why_not: TCC requires every participant to expose Try/Confirm/Cancel; this platform generates compensating sagas because a strangler extraction has participants (and a legacy monolith) that cannot be reshaped that way. Adopt it per participant where isolation is worth it.

considered.teaches: Split along DDD subdomains — core, supporting, generic — so the investment goes where the business differentiates.
considered.title: Decompose by subdomain (DDD)
considered.why_not: needs boundary_strategy = subdomain — you chose domain

considered.teaches: With one or two real contexts, enforce package boundaries in one binary instead of paying for a network.
considered.title: Modular monolith first
considered.why_not: needs at most 2 services — this run has 5

considered.teaches: Run old and new on the same input, compare, then switch — proof for logic where a wrong answer costs money.
considered.title: Parallel run
considered.why_not: needs migration_approach = parallel-run — you chose strangler

considered.teaches: At fleet scale, prove which service is calling — mesh mTLS or workload identity tokens, not network location.
considered.title: Service-to-service identity
considered.why_not: needs at least 6 services — this run has 5

considered.teaches: mTLS, retries and traffic policy in the platform — ambient/sidecarless meshes make it cheaper at fleet scale.
considered.title: Service mesh
considered.why_not: needs at least 6 services — this run has 5

considered.teaches: Helpers deployed beside each pod — fading for meshes, still used for agents and Dapr.
considered.title: Sidecar / ambassador
considered.why_not: Sidecarless (ambient / eBPF) meshes are displacing it, and nothing in this run scaffolds a sidecar.

considered.teaches: Domain package imports nothing infrastructural; adapters implement its ports — worth it only for a large, long-lived, infrastructure-heavy service.
considered.title: Hexagonal (ports and adapters)
considered.why_not: needs service_internal_structure = hexagonal — you chose flat-package

selected.teaches: When one screen needs three services, compose once at the edge with bounded fan-out — not three round-trips from the client.
selected.title: Gateway aggregation

selected.teaches: One edge for every client — routing, auth, rate limits and the strangler route table live there, not in each service.
selected.title: API gateway

selected.teaches: Each consumer pins what it reads from a provider; the provider’s CI fails when it would break a consumer — independent deploys stay safe.
selected.title: Contract testing

selected.because: you chose event_backbone = nats, which is not none
selected.teaches: The in-process bus becomes a broker: every topic a context publishes becomes a durable subject, published through the outbox.
selected.title: Event-driven messaging

selected.teaches: One coordinator owns the multi-service write: each step a local transaction, each failure a compensating step, the riskiest step last.
selected.title: Saga — orchestration

selected.teaches: Let the platform resolve names — compose service names, Kubernetes Services, Container Apps app names — and pass base URLs by environment.
selected.title: Service discovery

selected.teaches: Every cross-service read is a typed net/http client with a context deadline; gRPC is ported where the monolith already speaks it, not imposed.
selected.title: Synchronous transport — REST at the edge, gRPC inside

selected.teaches: Answer a cross-service query by calling the owners and joining in memory — try this before building a read model.
selected.title: API composition

selected.because: you chose orchestrator = azure-containerapps, which is not compose
selected.teaches: Pods × pool size must fit under the database’s max_connections — set it, don’t inherit a default.
selected.title: Connection-pool budget

selected.teaches: An aggregate is the consistency boundary; what it records as having happened is the event other services react to.
selected.title: Domain events and aggregates

selected.teaches: Two versions of the code always share the schema during a rollout — add, migrate, then remove, never rename in place.
selected.title: Expand–contract schema change

selected.teaches: The same guarantee at the HTTP edge — a caller-supplied key makes a retried write a no-op.
selected.title: Idempotency key

selected.because: you chose event_backbone = nats, which is not none
selected.teaches: At-least-once is reality — record each processed message id in the same transaction as its effect.
selected.title: Idempotent consumer

selected.teaches: A version column and a conditional UPDATE — the split widened every write window, and last-writer-wins now loses data.
selected.title: Optimistic concurrency

selected.because: you chose outbox = sql-outbox, which is not none
selected.teaches: Decide who drains the outbox — one relay per service, leader-elected or SKIP LOCKED — and make sure every replica is allowed to run it.
selected.title: Outbox relay topology

selected.teaches: A saga has no isolation — other requests see its intermediate states, so design semantic locks and reversible steps.
selected.title: Saga isolation countermeasures

selected.because: you chose outbox = sql-outbox, which is not none
selected.teaches: Write the row and the message in one local transaction, relay after commit — the only honest way out of the dual write.
selected.title: Transactional outbox

selected.teaches: Translate at every boundary — the consumer maps the provider’s contract into its own types, so one service’s model never leaks into another.
selected.title: Anti-corruption layer

selected.teaches: Put an interface in front of the in-process call, swap the implementation for a client behind it — the in-code half of the strangler.
selected.title: Branch by abstraction

selected.teaches: Each service owns its tables; nobody else reads them — the one invariant that makes independent deployment real.
selected.title: Database per service

selected.teaches: A service is a thing the business does and owns data for — catalog, orders, payments — never a technical layer.
selected.title: Decompose by business capability

selected.teaches: Extract a service only against a named force — team, scale, isolation or lifecycle; everything else stays in a bounded core.
selected.title: Right-sizing

selected.teaches: Put a gateway in front of the monolith and move one route group at a time; the monolith shrinks while production keeps working.
selected.title: Strangler fig

selected.teaches: Boundaries come from data ownership and co-writes measured in the shards; the model only refines names and edges it can be checked against.
selected.title: How the cut is computed

selected.teaches: Every service looks the same when you open it — cmd/, internal/, migrations/, one go.mod — so a reader learns the fleet once.
selected.title: Go microservice conventions

selected.teaches: One pinned stack, stated once — Go 1.26, a module per service in one go.work, slog + OpenTelemetry, NATS JetStream, distroless nonroot images.
selected.title: The 2026 Go target architecture

selected.teaches: One small shared startup path — config, slog, OTel, health, graceful shutdown — so every main.go is the same ten lines.
selected.title: Microservice chassis

selected.teaches: /healthz says the process lives; /readyz says it can serve — keep them different or the orchestrator restarts healthy pods.
selected.title: Health checks

selected.teaches: Traces, metrics and logs over one OTLP pipe; the trace id in every log line; the backend is a swap.
selected.title: Observability — slog + OpenTelemetry

selected.teaches: Configuration from the environment, secrets from the platform’s store via workload identity — never in git, never in the image.
selected.title: Secrets and configuration

selected.teaches: Validate the token at the gateway and again in each service; carry identity as a claim, not as an in-process context value.
selected.title: Security — JWT at the edge and in every service

selected.teaches: Test against real Postgres and NATS in containers, not mocks — the split moved the risk into the edges mocks hide.
selected.title: Integration testing with real dependencies

selected.because: you chose orchestrator = azure-containerapps, which is not compose
selected.teaches: Scale HTTP services on CPU/RPS and consumers on queue depth — CPU is the wrong signal for a JetStream consumer.
selected.title: Autoscaling — HPA and KEDA

selected.teaches: Prove the timeouts, breakers and compensations work by breaking things on purpose, in a test environment first.
selected.title: Chaos engineering

selected.teaches: One static binary per service in a distroless nonroot image, deployed the same way everywhere — compose locally, Kubernetes/Helm or Container Apps in production.
selected.title: Deployment — compose, Kubernetes, Azure Container Apps

selected.teaches: Move traffic to an extracted service gradually — weighted routes and flags, with a fast way back.
selected.title: Progressive delivery

selected.teaches: Limit at the edge per client, and inside services on expensive endpoints — shed load before the database does.
selected.title: Rate limiting

selected.teaches: Every hop has a deadline, bounded retries with jitter for idempotent calls, and a breaker per upstream.
selected.title: Resilience — timeouts, retries, breakers

selected.teaches: Keep the ported package as the unit — one package per context inside the service, wiring in cmd/, adapters beside it; Go rewards fewer layers.
selected.title: Flat package per context

selected.teaches: Omissions are decisions — plugin architectures, space-based grids, serverless-per-function and a shared-library "platform" are not targets here.
selected.title: Architecture styles this playbook does not apply
